overview: This map label covers parts of medieval Yemen from about 1000 to 1530, not one state lasting five centuries. Sulayhid rulers, Zaydi imams, Ayyubids, Rasulids and Tahirids held different territories at different times. The broad outline and its changing eastern edge cannot show those divisions accurately. The Rasulids were especially influential in the southern highlands, coastal plain and maritime trade.

periods.title: Regional rulers and the Sulayhid court
periods.summary: Yemen contained competing local powers. Queen Arwa’s Sulayhid court was one influential centre before her death in 1138.

periods.title: Ayyubid expansion
periods.summary: Ayyubid forces established rule in much of Yemen; this did not erase local political and religious communities.

periods.title: The Rasulid sultanate
periods.summary: From around 1228 or 1229, Rasulid rulers developed an influential southern state with extensive administrative and scholarly activity.

periods.title: Tahirid rule in Lower Yemen
periods.summary: The Tahirids replaced the Rasulids across much of Lower Yemen while facing northern Zaydi rivals.

periods.title: Several competing centres
periods.summary: After the Tahirid sultan’s defeat, Zaydi rulers, Tahirid remnants and military governors divided authority. The map stops during this unsettled period.

items.text: Queen Arwa, also known as Sayyida Hurra, moved the Sulayhid seat from Sanaa to Dhu Jibla. She built a palace and converted an older one into a mosque. Her future mother-in-law Asma had helped educate her and had herself participated in government. This was an exceptional courtly story of women exercising political and religious authority, not evidence of equal opportunities for every woman.

Ayyubid expansion began in the 1170s. The Rasulids emerged as independent rulers around 1228 or 1229 and remained powerful until 1454. Their records show officials organizing territory and markets, alongside scholars writing about history, astronomy, medicine and agriculture. Yet northern Zaydi leaders remained important rivals: one colour on this map hides a much more complicated political landscape.

Aden linked the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean. Ships and merchants connected Yemen to distant markets, and the Rasulids made overseas commerce an important part of their power. Inland agriculture and coastal exchange belonged to the same economy: the busy port depended on routes and communities beyond its harbour.

Farmers used more than one way to obtain water. Irrigation along major wadis worked alongside rainfall and the collection of runoff. A tax register compiled for the Rasulid sultan al-Muayyad, who died in 1321, even preserves a plan of irrigation along Wadi Zabid. Such records connect channels and fields with the government’s interest in harvests and revenue.

Al-Ashraf’s late-thirteenth-century farming book covered planting times, grain, pulses, fruit, fragrant plants, vegetables and pests. Royal interest could reach right into the garden. Rasulid horticultural experiments included roses and grapevines; agricultural learning was partly about practical cultivation, not only impressive books on a shelf.

Some crop names remembered a season. Medieval Rasulid sources describe a sorghum variety called baynt, planted in January and harvested in late March. Al-Afdal explained its name by planting between particular stars of the Great Bear. These were local timing traditions, and the elaborate twenty-eight-marker calendar documented much later should not be projected intact into medieval Yemen.

Long voyages affected the people left at home. Before travelling from Egypt to Yemen, the Jewish merchant Moses ben Yefet arranged money and wheat for his wife Sitt al-Fakhr, their family and a maidservant in Fustat. Their twelfth-century legal agreement specifies 25 dinars and five measures of wheat. He also provided a conditional divorce deed in case he failed to return.

Moses did reach Aden: his name appears on a letter sent from there in 1156. That letter described a ship lost on the voyage from Aden to India’s Malabar Coast. The documents reveal the risks behind commercial journeys and why families made careful legal arrangements. They survive because papers accumulated in a synagogue storeroom in Cairo.

A brass astrolabe made in Yemen in 1291 names the Rasulid prince Umar ibn Yusuf as its maker. The future sultan wrote about constructing scientific instruments, and a surviving manuscript includes his teachers’ certifications of his skill. An astrolabe brought measurements of the sky into work on time and prayer. Even a prince could need his teachers to sign off on his work.

A scientific text by al-Ashraf tells the maker of a compass bowl to label its rim “شمال جنوب مشرق مغرب”, meaning “north, south, east, west”. This Arabic sample follows Petra Schmidl’s normalized scholarly edition of a manuscript copied in Yemen in 1293, now in Cairo. The directions occur at folio 144v; they are words from an identified medieval witness, rather than a modern invented phrase.

Al-Ashraf’s compass used a magnetized steel needle crossed with a light plant stem and floated on water. His text explains how to protect it from wind and use its approximate alignment to work out the direction of prayer. The author valued a device that could function under clouds or at night, when sighting the sun or stars was difficult.

One fourteenth-century royal manuscript contains a remarkable six-language glossary: Arabic, Persian, Turkic, Greek, Armenian and Mongol, all written in Arabic letters. Vocabulary includes clothing, animals, foods and household equipment. It even explains chopsticks as two pieces of wood used for eating noodles. That entry reveals a compiler’s wide interests; it does not tell us that chopsticks sat on every Yemeni dinner table.

Zabid was an important centre of Islamic learning. UNESCO identifies fourteen surviving madrasas from the Rasulid period, with brick buildings and, in some cases, elaborate carved brick and stucco. Students came for religious knowledge and other sciences. The town’s institutions made education part of its urban identity, although their existence does not establish that every child attended school.

Books preserved interests in both plant and animal health. Al-Afdal’s agricultural treatise included medicinal plants, while al-Ashraf wrote a separate veterinary work that also discussed fodder crops such as sorghum. These texts show subjects that scholars investigated. They do not prove that every remedy worked or that every household could consult a trained practitioner.

The Tahirid ruler Amir ibn Abd al-Wahhab founded the Amiriya madrasa at Rada in 1504. Its complex combined a richly decorated, six-domed prayer space with living quarters and facilities for students. Water channels supplied the ablution area, and a large open basin stood beside the building. Keeping a school functioning involved water and accommodation as well as lessons.

Modern restoration of the Amiriya revived the making of qudad, a waterproof material using lime and crushed volcanic aggregate. Craftspeople tested mixtures when the exact proportions were no longer readily remembered. Conservators also uncovered painted decoration hidden beneath dust, soot and whitewash. The work recovered evidence of historical building skills while training a new generation of specialists.

The Tahirid defeat in 1517 did not bring all Yemen under one new government. Zaydi rulers expanded from the north, Tahirid remnants held Aden and some fortresses, and military governors based at Zabid claimed Ottoman allegiance. Coins of the last Tahirid prince at Aden include dates in 1529 and 1534. The latter is already beyond this record’s 1530 cutoff.

ending.text: The map’s 1530 endpoint is not Yemen’s disappearance or the end of one continuous kingdom. Rasulid power had ended in 1454, and the Tahirid sultan was killed in 1517 while smaller Tahirid authorities continued. Ottoman forces took Aden in 1538, beyond this map’s span; Zaydi power and Yemeni communities continued through changing regimes.
